alt: A tree diagram. The nervous system divides into the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord), which processes information and makes decisions, and the peripheral nervous system (all other nerves), which carries messages to and from the body. The peripheral system divides into the somatic system for voluntary movement and sensation and the autonomic system for involuntary functions such as heart rate, breathing and digestion.
caption: The CNS decides; the PNS carries messages. Somatic is voluntary, autonomic is involuntary.

after: ## The endocrine system and fight or flight
alt: The nervous system sends electrical messages along nerves; the endocrine system releases hormones into the blood, which is slower but longer lasting. The pituitary gland controls many glands and the adrenal glands release adrenaline. In fight or flight, a perceived threat activates the autonomic nervous system and adrenaline is released, raising heart and breathing rate, widening pupils, tensing muscles, increasing sweating and slowing digestion, until the threat passes.
caption: Adrenaline and the autonomic nervous system ready the body to fight or run.

after: ## The endocrine system and fight or flight
alt: Three steps in order: an event, then physiological arousal, then the brain's interpretation of that arousal, which is the emotion. Evaluation cards: panic after noticing a racing heart supports the theory; Cannon argued that bodily changes are too slow and that the same arousal occurs in different emotions such as fear and excitement.
caption: James-Lange: the body reacts first, and the emotion is our interpretation of that reaction.

alt: A message passes from heat receptors in the hand along a sensory neuron to the spinal cord, through a relay neuron, and along a motor neuron to the arm muscles, which contract. Cards give each neuron's location, job and structure: sensory has long dendrites and a short axon, relay has both short, motor has short dendrites and a long axon.
caption: Sensory neurons carry messages in, relay neurons connect, motor neurons carry messages out to act.

alt: A sending neuron's axon terminal holds vesicles of neurotransmitter. Five steps: the impulse arrives, neurotransmitters are released into the gap, they bind to receptors on the next neuron, the effect is excitatory or inhibitory, and leftover neurotransmitter is taken back by reuptake or broken down. The next neuron fires only if excitation outweighs inhibition overall.
caption: Electrical along the neuron, chemical across the gap; reuptake by the sending neuron ends the signal.

after: ## Hebb's theory of learning and neuronal growth
alt: Two pairs of neurons: before, a thin weak connection; after one repeatedly helps to fire the other, a thick, stronger and more efficient connection. Cards explain cell assemblies that represent a memory or skill, that practice makes pathways quicker to activate, and that rehearsal strengthens synaptic connections.
caption: Learning physically changes the brain: repeated firing strengthens connections.

after: ## Brain structure and localisation of function
alt: A schematic side view of the brain showing the frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes and the cerebellum. The motor area is at the back of the frontal lobe with Broca's area lower in the frontal lobe; the somatosensory area is at the front of the parietal lobe; the auditory area and Wernicke's area are in the temporal lobe; the visual area is in the occipital lobe.
caption: Specific areas carry out specific functions: Broca's is frontal, Wernicke's is temporal.

alt: Two study cards. Penfield stimulated the brain surface of awake epilepsy patients with a weak current; stimulating parts of the temporal lobe sometimes produced vivid experiences, though the patients were not typical. Tulving's small group was injected with radioactive gold; episodic thinking was linked to the front of the cortex and semantic thinking to the back, though the sample was tiny.
caption: Both studies support localisation, but both used small or unusual samples.

alt: Four rows linking damaged areas to effects: the motor area on one side causes weakness or paralysis on the opposite side; Broca's area causes slow, effortful speech with understanding intact; Wernicke's area causes fluent but meaningless speech and poor understanding; the frontal lobe can change personality and self-control.
caption: Damage effects follow localisation: the area hit predicts the ability lost.
